question: Articles 21 and 22 TEU provide that it is for the Council to define the strategic interests and objectives of the Union’s external action.

Under the Common Foreign and Security Policy, implementation and external representation are, in principle, the responsibility of the VP/HR (Article 27 TEU), whilst, under Article 17 TEU, the Commission President represents the Commission in matters falling within her own competences, such as trade, development cooperation and humanitarian aid.

In practice, however, there appears to be an increasingly frequent overlap or lack of clarity in the division of roles, particularly in the context of the socalled ‘Team Europe’ approach, whereby the Commission President also adopts external political positions vis-à-vis third countries. 1.

How does the Council interpret the division of competences under the Treaty between the Commission President and the VP/HR, on the one hand, and the European Council, on the other, with regard to public or diplomatic positions vis-à-vis third countries?
How does the Council ensure that the Commission President does not, in external dealings, adopt positions that fall within the Council’s exclusive competence under the CFSP?
To what extent does the ‘Team Europe’ approach influence the practical division of roles between the Commission President, the VP/HR and the Council when it comes to the Union’s external action?
answer: The division of competences between the EU institutions is enshrined in the Treaties. In respect of CFSP, Article 24 TEU clearly prescribes that “the common foreign and security policy is subject to specific rules and procedures”.

On the one hand, it is for the European Council to define the general political direction and priorities of the Union and for the Council to define the policy of the Union vis-à-vis third countries and international organisations.

Specifically, the European Council shall provide the Union with the necessary impetus for its development and shall define the general political directions and priorities thereof (Article 15(1) TEU), while the Council shall carry out policymaking and coordinating functions (Article 16(1) TEU).

Specifically regarding common foreign and security policy, this shall be defined and implemented by the European Council and the Council (Article 24(1), second subparagraph TEU, and further elaborated in Articles 26 and 29 TEU).

On the other hand, it is for the Commission to ensure the external representation of the Union (Article 17(1) TEU) vis-à-vis third countries, with the exception of common foreign and security policy, for which Article 27(2) TEU provides that the High Representative shall represent the Union, and other cases provided for in the Treaties.

In the exercise of their powers, the EU institutions are bound by Article 13(2) TEU. Under that provision, each EU institution is to act within the limits of the powers conferred on it by the Treaties, and in conformity with the procedures, conditions and objectives set out in them.

That provision reflects the principle of institutional balance, characteristic of the institutional structure of the European Union, a principle which requires that each of the institutions must exercise its powers with due regard for the powers of the other institutions.
Once a position on a foreign policy matter has been agreed in the Council, all Member States and institutional actors are bound to uphold and defend this position on the international scene.
